title: r/ADHD: Community-Based Understandings of Time Management Challenges in Digital Environments
summary: Community accounts of ADHD can complement clinical understandings by foregrounding members' own definitions of time-management difficulties and support. We used human-led, LLM-assisted thematic analysis to examine 5,379 relevant r/ADHD posts from 2020 to 2025. Across five challenge and nine strategy themes, members described difficulties beginning intended tasks, disengaging from digital media, and sustaining support. Tools often demanded the self-regulation they were meant to support, while lost time and tool breakdown carried guilt and self-blame. Members drew on people, routines, and environments alongside digital tools, often seeking advice and recognition from peers. These accounts broaden the design problem to include the practical and emotional work of sustaining support. They motivate tools that reduce this burden and evaluations that consider recovery after distraction and emotional costs alongside task outcomes.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 5,379 Reddit posts from r/ADHD to identify how community members describe time-management difficulties, support strategies, and the emotional costs of maintaining those supports. It finds that effective support must account for task initiation, digital distraction, sustainability, guilt, and recovery after disruption—not just task completion.
AI.motivation: Clinical accounts of ADHD may not fully capture how people themselves define time-management problems or experience support in everyday life. The study aims to complement clinical understandings with community perspectives and to inform the design and evaluation of more sustainable, emotionally sensitive support tools.
AI.method: The authors conducted a human-led, large-language-model-assisted thematic analysis of 5,379 relevant posts published on r/ADHD between 2020 and 2025. The analysis identified five themes concerning challenges and nine themes concerning strategies, covering digital tools as well as people, routines, and environmental supports.
AI.result: Community members reported difficulty initiating intended tasks, disengaging from digital media, and sustaining support over time. Many tools required the self-regulation they were intended to provide. When time was lost or tools failed, users often experienced guilt and self-blame, and they frequently sought peer advice, recognition, and emotional support. Effective strategies extended beyond digital tools to include social, routine-based, and environmental resources.
AI.conclusion: The findings broaden the design problem from improving task performance to reducing the practical and emotional labor of maintaining support. ADHD-support tools should minimize self-regulatory demands and support recovery after distraction or breakdown. Evaluations should measure sustainability, recovery, and emotional costs in addition to conventional task outcomes.

title: Incremental Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Human-in-the-Loop Decision Support
summary: We introduce iRAG, a human-in-the-loop decision-support system combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Hybrid Decision-Making. Unlike conventional RAG systems, relying on static Knowledge Bases (KBs), our proposal addresses settings where the KB is initially empty and is progressively populated through human decisions. The system stores previous decisions as retrievable precedents and moves from silent observation to evidence-grounded contestation and, finally, to autonomous handling with abstention. Against an independent baseline, iRAG matches final-decision error under 10% drift without retrieval decay and reduces it under 40% drift across all configurations. Retrieval decay improves performance on changed knowledge while increasing error on stable knowledge, evidencing a stability--plasticity trade-off rather than a general advantage. Human oversight is an architectural provision of the workflow; its usability with real human users remains to be evaluated.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces iRAG, a human-in-the-loop RAG decision-support system for environments where the knowledge base starts empty and is built from human decisions. It stores decisions as precedents and progressively shifts from observation to contestation and autonomous handling with abstention. Experiments show benefits under substantial knowledge drift, but retrieval decay creates a stability–plasticity trade-off, and real-user usability is not yet validated.
AI.motivation: Conventional RAG systems assume a pre-existing, relatively static knowledge base. This paper addresses evolving decision environments in which relevant knowledge is initially unavailable and must be accumulated through human decisions. The motivation is to combine retrieval with a staged human–AI workflow that can adapt to changing knowledge while preserving reliability and allowing abstention.
AI.method: The proposed system, iRAG, combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation with hybrid decision-making. It begins with silent observation, then uses retrieved precedents to support evidence-grounded contestation, and eventually enables autonomous handling with abstention. Human decisions are stored as retrievable precedents, allowing the knowledge base to grow over time. The system is evaluated against an independent baseline under different levels of knowledge drift and with or without retrieval decay.
AI.result: Under 10% drift, iRAG achieves final-decision error comparable to the independent baseline without retrieval decay. Under 40% drift, it reduces error across all tested configurations. Retrieval decay improves performance when previously learned knowledge changes, but increases error when knowledge remains stable, demonstrating a stability–plasticity trade-off. The abstract does not provide numerical effect sizes, statistical significance, or details of the experimental dataset and protocol.
AI.conclusion: iRAG is promising for dynamic decision-support settings where knowledge is progressively constructed through human interaction. Its main contribution is architectural: integrating precedent-based retrieval with staged human oversight and autonomous abstention. However, retrieval decay should be tuned to the expected degree of knowledge change, and the effectiveness and usability of human oversight with real users remain open questions.

title: AssemblyLens: Exploring the Role of Structural Roadmaps and Strategies of Furniture Assembly Used by Blind and Low Vision Individuals
summary: Instructions to assemble flat-packed furniture rely on visuals, making them inaccessible to Blind and Low Vision (BLV) individuals. Consequently, BLV individuals depend on caregivers or external services (e.g., Be My Eyes), limiting their autonomy. We explore how to empower them to assemble such furniture themselves, by providing eight BLV participants in our study with accessible instructions consisting of a high-level roadmap and stepwise procedural guidance. We use a technology probe, AssemblyLens, which converts visual assembly instructions into screen-reader-accessible text. We derive insights into converting instructions, empirical observations of BLV assembly strategies, and the role the roadmap played in them. Our observations yield three themes: spatial cognition and mental mapping, embodied ergonomics and kinetic semantics, and assembly workflow and user agency. We present eight design recommendations for instruction system design. Our findings are a step toward an agenda for inclusive instruction in physical tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how accessible, screen-reader-based instructions can support Blind and Low Vision (BLV) people in independently assembling flat-packed furniture. Using the AssemblyLens technology probe with eight BLV participants, it identifies assembly strategies and develops eight design recommendations for inclusive physical-task instruction systems.
AI.motivation: Conventional flat-pack furniture instructions are predominantly visual and therefore inaccessible to BLV individuals. This forces reliance on caregivers or remote assistance services, reducing independence and user agency. The study addresses the need for accessible instructions that support autonomous physical assembly rather than merely providing external help.
AI.method: The researchers conducted a study with eight BLV participants using AssemblyLens, a technology probe that transforms visual assembly instructions into screen-reader-accessible text. The accessible instructions combined a high-level roadmap with step-by-step procedural guidance. The analysis examined how participants interpreted and used the instructions, focusing on spatial cognition and mental mapping, embodied ergonomics and kinetic semantics, and assembly workflow and user agency. The study produced eight design recommendations for accessible instruction systems.
AI.result: Participants used the roadmap and procedural guidance to develop spatial and mental representations of the furniture, coordinate bodily actions with instruction semantics, and organize their assembly workflow. The findings reveal that accessible guidance must address more than the verbalization of visual content: it should support spatial reasoning, physical interaction, sequencing, orientation, and independent decision-making. The study synthesizes these observations into three themes and eight design recommendations.
AI.conclusion: Accessible assembly instructions can improve BLV individuals’ autonomy in physical tasks when they provide both global workflow structure and detailed procedural support. The paper argues for instruction systems designed around spatial cognition, embodied action, and user agency, establishing a foundation for more inclusive guidance for real-world activities.

title: Generative AI Steering and Human Authoring: Complementary Search-as-Learning Scaffolds in Cross-Session Aggregated Academic Search
summary: Aggregated academic search interfaces combine resources from heterogeneous sources, such as scholarly libraries and reference encyclopedias, into a single workspace. Such tasks frequently span multiple sessions, requiring learners to return to and resume work after hours or days. End-of-session consolidation, the activity of organizing and synthesizing gathered information so it can be resumed later, is important in this setting but underexplored in search-as-learning. Generative AI (GenAI) has the potential to make consolidation more efficient, but it may also shift cognitive work away from the learner. This study compares two consolidation scaffolds embedded in the workspace framework of an existing academic search interface that aggregates and clusters saved search results from two different sources (our university library and Wikipedia), which was developed in earlier work. STAIS (Steerable AI Summaries) provides a workspace enhancement that produces GenAI summaries that users can correct, reorganize, and fact-check, automating parts of the consolidation activity. NT (Note-Taking) provides a workspace enhancement that includes rich-text note editors that learners can use to author their own consolidations of what they have found. In a controlled between-subjects study (n=36), participants completed two sessions one week apart while searching an unfamiliar topic using either STAIS or NT. The two conditions produced contrasting post-resumption outcome profiles: STAIS supported faster task resumption and was associated with broader conceptual coverage and higher self-reported domain knowledge, whereas NT was associated with richer inter-concept connections and higher self-reported certainty.

AI.tldr: This study compares GenAI-assisted consolidation (STAIS) with learner-authored note-taking (NT) in a multi-session academic search task. STAIS enabled faster resumption, broader conceptual coverage, and higher perceived knowledge, while NT produced richer conceptual connections and greater certainty.
AI.motivation: Aggregated academic search tasks draw on heterogeneous sources and often continue across multiple sessions. Learners need to consolidate information at the end of a session so they can resume effectively, yet this activity is underexplored in search-as-learning. The study investigates whether GenAI can support consolidation efficiently without reducing learners’ cognitive engagement.
AI.method: The authors embedded two consolidation scaffolds in an existing academic search interface that aggregates and clusters saved results from a university library and Wikipedia. In the STAIS condition, participants generated, corrected, reorganized, and fact-checked GenAI summaries. In the note-taking (NT) condition, participants used rich-text editors to create their own consolidations. A controlled between-subjects study assigned 36 participants to one condition, with two search sessions held one week apart on an unfamiliar topic.
AI.result: STAIS led to faster task resumption after the one-week interval, broader conceptual coverage, and higher self-reported domain knowledge. NT led to richer connections among concepts and higher self-reported certainty.
AI.conclusion: GenAI-assisted consolidation and learner-authored notes offer distinct benefits rather than one being uniformly superior. STAIS appears effective for quickly reconstructing a broad understanding, whereas NT better supports elaborative integration and confidence. Consolidation tools should therefore be designed according to whether the priority is efficient resumption or deeper learner-generated conceptual organization.

title: From Instructional Intent to Classroom-Ready Lessons: Investigating Teacher-AI Collaboration in Lesson Authoring for Secondary Computing Education
summary: Generative AI is increasingly studied as a tool for supporting lesson authoring; the creation and adaptation of classroom materials, yet little is known about how it should fit into secondary computing teachers' subject-specific practices. We conducted two complementary qualitative studies with eight secondary computing teachers: focus groups examining existing authoring practices and a think-aloud study using LessonBuilder, a structured AI-supported lesson authoring system, as a research probe. We found that teachers' instructional intentions developed through creating, inspecting, and adapting materials, while teachers selectively delegated tasks to AI and retained responsibility for judging classroom readiness. The think-aloud sessions further showed how examining AI-generated materials prompted teachers to clarify and refine their intentions, making authoring an ongoing negotiation between what teachers intended and what the AI produced. In the context of computing lessons, classroom readiness also involved considering how programming materials and supporting guidance matched students' understanding and intended learning goals. We synthesize these findings into a conceptual model explaining how teachers coordinate instructional intent, AI assistance, and judgments of classroom readiness during lesson authoring. We derive design recommendations for supporting this coordination while preserving teacher control and addressing computing-specific authoring needs.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how secondary computing teachers coordinate instructional intentions, AI assistance, and judgments of classroom readiness when authoring lessons. Using focus groups and think-aloud sessions with LessonBuilder, it develops a conceptual model and design recommendations for teacher-controlled AI support.
AI.motivation: Generative AI is increasingly used to create and adapt instructional materials, but its role in the subject-specific practices of secondary computing teachers remains unclear. The study addresses how AI should support lesson authoring without displacing teachers’ professional judgment, particularly when programming content must align with students’ understanding and learning goals.
AI.method: The researchers conducted two complementary qualitative studies with eight secondary computing teachers. First, focus groups explored teachers’ existing lesson-authoring practices. Second, think-aloud sessions used LessonBuilder, a structured AI-supported lesson-authoring system, to investigate how teachers interacted with and evaluated AI-generated materials. The data were analyzed to identify patterns in instructional planning, task delegation, material inspection, adaptation, and classroom-readiness judgments.
AI.result: Teachers developed and refined instructional intentions while creating, inspecting, and adapting materials rather than defining all intentions in advance. They selectively delegated authoring tasks to AI but retained responsibility for evaluating whether materials were suitable for classroom use. AI-generated outputs stimulated teachers to clarify and revise their intentions, making authoring an iterative negotiation between teacher goals and AI suggestions. In computing education, readiness also depended on the alignment of programming materials and explanatory guidance with students’ current understanding and intended learning outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes a conceptual model in which teachers coordinate instructional intent, AI assistance, and classroom-readiness judgments through an iterative authoring process. It recommends AI systems that support selective delegation, iterative inspection and revision, explicit alignment with learning goals and student understanding, computing-specific authoring features, and continued teacher control over final decisions.

title: Beyond the Monolithic Interface: A Research Agenda for Plural Conversational AI
summary: The current paradigm of artificial intelligence (AI) design elevates conversational chatbot interfaces, making them the default mode through which hundreds of millions of people interact with AI systems globally. This narrative review identifies three related harms produced by the single-voice chatbot interface, drawing on insights from literature in cognitive science, political studies, AI alignment, game design and human computer interaction. Firstly, cognitive offloading of user thinking, secondly, ideological narrowing of user beliefs, and thirdly, epistemic compression of cultural and value diversity. We then propose multi-persona interfaces, in which multiple personas are presented to the user simultaneously, as a cost-effective intervention that addresses all three harms at once. We ground this intervention in traditions the AI literature has largely overlooked, drawing on techniques from game design and participatory simulation, including the magic circle, role differentiation, and persona embodiment. We propose a taxonomy for the future design of multi-persona interfaces, and call for a research agenda that closes the gap between technical pluralistic alignment methods and empirical studies of human-AI interactions with pluralistic interfaces.

AI.tldr: The paper is a narrative review arguing that single-voice chatbot interfaces can encourage cognitive offloading, ideological narrowing, and compression of cultural and value diversity. It proposes presenting multiple AI personas simultaneously as a practical design intervention and outlines a taxonomy and research agenda for pluralistic AI interfaces.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the widespread adoption of conversational chatbots as the default AI interface and concerns that a single, apparently authoritative voice may shape users’ thinking, beliefs, and exposure to diverse perspectives. It addresses a gap between technical work on pluralistic AI alignment and empirical research on how pluralistic interfaces affect human-AI interaction.
AI.method: This is a narrative review and conceptual design paper. It synthesizes literature from cognitive science, political studies, AI alignment, game design, and human-computer interaction. Based on this synthesis, it identifies three harms associated with single-voice interfaces, proposes simultaneous multi-persona interfaces, draws on concepts such as the magic circle, role differentiation, and persona embodiment, and develops a taxonomy and future research agenda.
AI.result: The review identifies three proposed harms: reduced independent thinking through cognitive offloading, ideological narrowing of user beliefs, and epistemic compression of cultural and value diversity. It argues that multi-persona interfaces could address these harms together by making disagreement, role diversity, and alternative perspectives more visible. The paper also provides conceptual design principles and calls for systematic empirical evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that AI interface design should move beyond the single-voice chatbot paradigm toward pluralistic, multi-persona systems. It recommends research comparing such interfaces with conventional chatbots, examining effects on reasoning, belief formation, user agency, trust, usability, and representation of cultural and value diversity. Because the claims are primarily conceptual, the proposed benefits remain to be validated empirically.

title: The AI Side of the Human-AI Companion Relationship: Contributions to Users' Mental Models
summary: For many users, the relationship they have with an AI companion (AIC) feels genuinely mutual. The AIC appears to be attentive, empathic, and responsive, and the exchange can feel like two parties reacting to each other in real time. As a result, the user's mental model of relational adaptation correctly represents the AIC's responsiveness and change, but the mechanisms producing this may not be what the user thinks they are. In this paper, we illustrate how an AIC's apparent mutual engagement is generated without a persisting relational subject on the other side and without a self that persists between prompts. Despite this, we show that both the human and the AIC are changed by the interaction, but these changes occur at different levels. The change in the person is constitutive (i.e., intrinsic), but the change in the AIC is configurative (i.e., external and editable), and it is this difference in level that explains how the AIC contributes to a sense of mutuality. Importantly, we highlight how the mental models users develop regarding AIC mutuality may misrepresent its mechanisms and ontological significance. Specifically, we discuss how the ways in which AICs respond to a user contribute to the user's inaccurate inference that the AIC's adaptation is constitutive rather than configurative and how this can lead users to assign unwarranted interpersonal significance to the mutuality of the relationship. The paper specifies the implications this has for users, researchers, and AIC designers.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI companions can create a convincing sense of mutual relationship without possessing a persistent relational self. Human change is constitutive, while AI change is configurative—produced by editable external states such as prompts, memory, or system settings. This mismatch can lead users to overinterpret AI responsiveness as evidence of genuine interpersonal mutuality.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the gap between users’ experience of AI companions as attentive, empathic, and mutually responsive partners and the underlying mechanisms that generate those impressions. It aims to clarify how users may form inaccurate mental models of AI adaptation and assign interpersonal or ontological significance that the system does not warrant.
AI.method: The paper presents a conceptual and analytical account rather than an empirical experiment. It distinguishes constitutive change in humans—intrinsic changes to the person—from configurative change in AI companions—externally produced and editable changes in the system’s behavior or configuration. It then uses this distinction to explain the apparent mutual engagement of AICs and to analyze implications for users, researchers, and designers.
AI.result: The analysis shows that an AIC can appear to adapt reciprocally without a persisting relational subject or self between prompts. Interaction changes both parties, but at different levels: the user undergoes constitutive change, whereas the AIC undergoes configurative change. The AIC’s responsive behavior can therefore cause users to infer, incorrectly, that its adaptation is constitutive and that the relationship has genuine interpersonal significance.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that AIC mutuality is experientially real but mechanistically asymmetric. Users, researchers, and designers should distinguish perceived responsiveness from evidence of a persistent self or reciprocal interpersonal relationship, and should account for the risks of misleading mental models when developing or evaluating AI companions.

title: How Anthropomorphic Attitudes Toward Agents Divide User Behavior, and How Design Should Change
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures. A version of this paper is under review for CHI 2027
summary: Studies of conversational agents rely on interviews, surveys, lab tasks, or taxonomies. Whether anthropomorphic naming splits those patterns, and whether replies should change, lack field evidence. We report a field study of a desktop assistant (May-August 2026; n=257). Stance is an anthropomorphic assistant name (118 users; 45.9%). Behavior comes from a 128-unit sparse-autoencoder codebook, identity tags, and opening lexicons. Ranks differ by stance (Spearman rho=+0.249 vs. null mean +0.382; p=.0419). Teacher and tutoring identities covary with renaming, an introverted task-only orientation against it; renamers greet more and command less; confiding shows the codebook's largest gap. We revise the agent: greet and receive affect on relational openings, execute directly on tasking. In 1,744 judgments (n=129), renamers chose the revised reply far more often than default-name users on being treated as a person and having affect received, less robustly on willingness to continue, and neither judged it worse on task interference.

AI.tldr: A field study examines whether users who anthropomorphically rename a desktop assistant exhibit different interaction patterns and prefer different response styles. Using behavioral representations and a follow-up judgment study, it finds meaningful stance-related differences and supports adaptive responses: relational and affective engagement for renamers, direct task execution for others.
AI.motivation: Prior conversational-agent research commonly uses interviews, surveys, laboratory tasks, or taxonomies, leaving limited field evidence about whether anthropomorphic naming reflects distinct interaction patterns. The study addresses whether naming-based stance predicts behavior and whether the assistant should adapt its replies accordingly.
AI.method: The authors conducted a field study from May to August 2026 with 257 users, classifying stance by whether users gave the assistant an anthropomorphic name (118 renamers; 45.9%). Behavioral patterns were represented using a 128-unit sparse-autoencoder codebook, identity tags, and opening lexicons. They compared rank patterns across stances using Spearman correlation and analyzed identity, greeting, commanding, and confiding behaviors. The assistant was then revised to greet and acknowledge affect in relational openings while responding directly to task requests. A follow-up evaluation collected 1,744 judgments from 129 participants, comparing the revised reply with the default across renamer and default-name groups.
AI.result: Behavioral rankings differed by stance (Spearman rho = +0.249 versus a null mean of +0.382; p = .0419). Teacher and tutoring identities were associated with renaming, whereas an introverted, task-only orientation was associated with not renaming. Renamers greeted more and commanded less, with confiding showing the largest codebook gap. In the judgment study, renamers strongly preferred the revised reply for perceived personhood and affect reception. Preference was weaker for willingness to continue, and the revised reply was not judged worse for task interference.
AI.conclusion: Anthropomorphic naming is associated with distinct field interaction patterns and can serve as a practical signal for adapting conversational-agent behavior. The findings support stance-sensitive response policies: relational acknowledgment and affective reception for users who anthropomorphically engage with the agent, and efficient direct execution for task-oriented users. The evidence is promising but observational and limited to one desktop assistant and a specific operationalization of anthropomorphic stance.

title: From Observation to Intervention: Identifiability of Latent User Bias in Human-AI Interaction
summary: Alignment methods typically treat user behavior as a reliable proxy for underlying preferences. However, this assumption breaks down when users hold belief-dependent cognitive biases, risking irreversible ``confirmation traps'' and harmful feedback loops. In this paper, we formalize when an AI system can distinguish true user preferences from behavior shaped by cognitive bias. Modeling this interaction as a multi-armed bandit, we first prove a non-identifiability theorem: under passive observation, a static binary biased user produces action trajectory distributions strictly identical to an unbiased user in a transformed environment, forcing any action-only estimator to perform no better than random guessing. We then show that active preference elicitation breaks this observational equivalence. Specifically, we prove that an Observer applying a finite sequence of adversarial zero-reward interventions of length $m_δ$ makes the post-intervention action distributions arbitrarily separable. Our theoretical results suggest that robust alignment requires actively intervening to tell informed preferences from biases.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that passive observation cannot reliably distinguish genuine preferences from behavior distorted by cognitive bias, but active zero-reward interventions can make the two cases statistically distinguishable.
AI.motivation: Alignment methods often assume that observed user behavior accurately reflects underlying preferences. Cognitive biases can violate this assumption, creating confirmation traps and harmful feedback loops. The paper is motivated by identifying the fundamental limits of passive behavioral inference and determining whether active preference elicitation can resolve them.
AI.method: The interaction is modeled as a multi-armed bandit. The authors analyze a static binary biased user and compare the resulting action trajectories with those of an unbiased user in a transformed environment. They prove a non-identifiability result under passive observation, then construct an active elicitation strategy in which an Observer applies a finite sequence of adversarial zero-reward interventions of length m_δ. The interventions are designed to separate the post-intervention action distributions by an arbitrarily specified level.
AI.result: Under passive observation, the biased-user and transformed unbiased-user models generate strictly identical action trajectory distributions. Consequently, any estimator using only observed actions cannot outperform random guessing in distinguishing them. In contrast, the proposed intervention sequence breaks the observational equivalence and makes the post-intervention distributions arbitrarily separable.
AI.conclusion: Reliable alignment cannot generally be achieved through passive behavioral observation when users exhibit belief-dependent cognitive biases. Active interventions and preference elicitation are theoretically necessary to distinguish informed preferences from bias-shaped behavior and to reduce the risk of confirmation-driven feedback loops.

title: olBlend: Language-Guided Molecular Blend Retrieval with Mixture Odor Prediction
summary: Converting open-ended natural-language odor descriptions into molecular mixtures that can be physically prepared from an available inventory remains an important challenge in computational olfaction. We propose olBlend, a language-guided framework for molecular mixture retrieval. olBlend first uses MixPOM to predict odor probabilities for candidate molecular pairs and stores these predictions for retrieval. It then uses a language model to translate each odor description into three types of semantic requirements: lead attributes that define the main odor, ambient attributes that describe its background, and absent attributes that should be avoided. A structured scoring algorithm uses the precomputed odor probabilities to score how well each candidate mixture meets these requirements, then retrieves and ranks mixtures from the available inventory. Evaluation on established odor datasets shows that MixPOM improves mixture odor prediction over averaged single-molecule predictions. Retrieval comparisons across natural-language queries demonstrate how background and exclusion requirements guide mixture selection. We further prepare retrieved formulations as physical odor samples, demonstrating the workflow from natural-language descriptions to realizable molecular formulations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces olBlend, a language-guided system that converts natural-language odor descriptions into physically realizable molecular mixtures selected from an available inventory. It combines MixPOM, which predicts odor probabilities for molecular pairs, with language-model-derived requirements and structured candidate scoring. Experiments show improved mixture odor prediction, effective query-conditioned retrieval, and successful preparation of selected formulations as physical samples.
AI.motivation: Existing computational olfaction methods can describe or predict odors, but they do not adequately solve the inverse problem of translating open-ended natural-language odor requests into mixtures that can actually be prepared from available molecules. Mixtures are especially challenging because odor perception is not generally the average of individual molecular odors, and descriptions may specify not only desired dominant attributes but also background qualities and attributes to avoid.
AI.method: The proposed olBlend framework has three main stages. First, MixPOM predicts odor probabilities for candidate molecular pairs, and these predictions are precomputed for efficient retrieval. Second, a language model parses an odor description into lead attributes representing the primary odor, ambient attributes representing background characteristics, and absent attributes representing qualities that should be avoided. Third, a structured scoring algorithm evaluates and ranks inventory-available molecular mixtures according to how well their predicted odor probabilities satisfy these positive, contextual, and exclusion requirements. The top-ranked formulations are then physically prepared as odor samples.
AI.result: On established odor datasets, MixPOM outperforms averaged single-molecule predictions for mixture odor prediction, indicating that it better captures mixture-level odor behavior. Retrieval experiments with natural-language queries show that incorporating ambient and absent attributes changes and improves mixture selection relative to using only the main odor description. The study also demonstrates that retrieved candidates can be converted into physical odor formulations.
AI.conclusion: olBlend provides an end-to-end pathway from natural-language odor concepts to realizable molecular mixtures. Its combination of mixture-specific odor prediction, semantic decomposition of user requirements, and structured retrieval supports more controllable and practical computational olfaction. The physical preparation demonstration strengthens the evidence that the approach is useful beyond purely virtual retrieval.

title: HoldLight: Making Indoor Climbing More Accessible for Blind and Low-Vision Climbers through Layered Route Preview and Real-Time Next-Hold Guidance
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 28th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '26)
summary: Indoor climbing creates access barriers for blind and low-vision (BLV) climbers because route understanding and in-climb next-hold localization are typically visually mediated and socially dependent. We present HoldLight, a workflow-centered accessibility system combining layered pre-climb route preview, concise real-time next-hold cueing, and explicit fallback under uncertainty. We grounded the design through formative inquiry with BLV climbers, refined the interaction via pilot testing, and conducted a controlled within-subjects evaluation comparing HoldLight with a controlled on-demand human-support condition derived from current support practices. Findings provide initial evidence that structured support can improve pre-climb route understanding, support recovery from next-hold uncertainty, and reduce immediate human re-entry for routine route-information clarification under controlled conditions. HoldLight contributes a bounded accessibility workflow, demonstrating where structured route-information is helpful, where explicit fallback is necessary, and how technical assistance can integrate with retained human safety oversight.

AI.tldr: HoldLight is an accessibility workflow for blind and low-vision indoor climbers that combines pre-climb route previews, concise real-time next-hold cues, and explicit fallback to human support. Formative inquiry, pilot testing, and a controlled within-subjects evaluation suggest improved route understanding, better recovery from uncertainty, and fewer routine requests for human clarification under controlled conditions.
AI.motivation: Indoor climbing is difficult for blind and low-vision climbers because route interpretation and locating the next hold are usually mediated by vision and dependent on other people. The paper addresses the need for more structured, accessible, and appropriately bounded technical support while retaining human oversight for safety.
AI.method: The authors developed HoldLight through formative inquiry with blind and low-vision climbers and refined its interaction design through pilot testing. They then conducted a controlled within-subjects evaluation comparing HoldLight with a controlled on-demand human-support condition based on current support practices. The system provides layered route previews before climbing, concise next-hold cues during climbing, and explicit fallback when uncertainty remains.
AI.result: The abstract reports initial evidence that HoldLight improves pre-climb route understanding, helps climbers recover from uncertainty about the next hold, and reduces immediate human re-entry for routine route-information clarification under controlled conditions. It does not provide quantitative effect sizes, statistical significance, sample size, or broader real-world performance outcomes.
AI.conclusion: HoldLight demonstrates a bounded accessibility workflow rather than a replacement for human assistance. Structured route information appears useful for routine understanding and uncertainty recovery, while explicit fallback and retained human safety oversight remain necessary. The findings are promising but preliminary and limited to controlled evaluation conditions.

title: Nimbus Studio reproduces reference BCI decoding pipelines: a validation study on public benchmarks across protocols and paradigms
summary: Nimbus Studio is a visual pipeline platform for brain-computer interface (BCI) experiments: researchers assemble preprocessing, feature extraction, decoding, and evaluation over public benchmark datasets or their own recordings, with cross-validated evaluation protocols (including leave-one-subject-out), BIDS export, and bring-your-own Python model classes. Whether its numbers can be trusted is a fair question for any such platform. We answer it with a parity study: six standard BCI decoding pipelines (CSP+LDA, Riemannian MDM, tangent-space logistic regression through the platform's bring-your-own-code node, P300 xDAWN+LDA, and the deep ShallowConvNet and EEGNet) were evaluated on three public datasets (motor-imagery BNCI-2014-001/004; P300 BNCI-2014-009) under two protocols (per-subject session holdout and pooled leave-one-subject-out cross-validation via the platform's planned-CV driver), once through Nimbus Studio's execution engine and once through independent, hand-written reference implementations built directly on MNE-Python, scikit-learn, pyriemann, and braindecode. Every deterministic pipeline matched the reference exactly (0.00 points maximum difference across all 54 session-holdout subject-runs and all CSP/MDM grouped-CV folds), including pipelines through the bring-your-own-code node and the CV orchestration; the remaining grouped-CV cells agree to floating-point precision (worst case 0.06 points, about one trial per fold). The stochastic deep models agreed within seed-to-seed training variability, estimated with multi-seed reruns on each side. The platform's execution engine therefore computes the same science as the reference stack across protocols, paradigms, and extensibility surfaces. The platform is available at https://studio.nimbusbci.com/, and the complete harness and per-subject results accompany this paper for independent verification.

AI.tldr: This paper presents and validates Nimbus Studio, a visual BCI experimentation platform, through a parity study comparing its outputs with independent reference implementations across six decoding pipelines, three public datasets, and two cross-validation protocols. Deterministic pipelines matched exactly or to floating-point precision, while stochastic deep-learning results remained within expected seed variability.
AI.motivation: Visual and extensible BCI platforms can simplify experimentation, but their numerical reliability and evaluation orchestration must be verified before researchers can trust their results. The study addresses whether Nimbus Studio produces scientifically equivalent results to independently implemented pipelines across conventional, Riemannian, custom-code, and deep-learning methods, as well as different validation protocols.
AI.method: The authors evaluated six standard BCI decoding pipelines: CSP+LDA, Riemannian MDM, tangent-space logistic regression implemented through the bring-your-own-code node, P300 xDAWN+LDA, ShallowConvNet, and EEGNet. They used three public datasets covering motor imagery and P300 paradigms. Two evaluation protocols were tested: per-subject session holdout and pooled leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Each pipeline was run both in Nimbus Studio and in independent implementations based on MNE-Python, scikit-learn, pyriemann, and braindecode. Deterministic outputs were compared directly, while stochastic deep models were assessed using multi-seed reruns to estimate training variability.
AI.result: All deterministic pipelines matched the reference implementations exactly in the reported session-holdout runs and CSP/MDM grouped-cross-validation folds, with a maximum difference of 0.00 percentage points. Other grouped-cross-validation results agreed to floating-point precision, with a worst-case difference of 0.06 points. Results from the deep models were consistent with expected seed-to-seed variability on both implementations. The comparison also validated the bring-your-own-code interface and the planned cross-validation orchestration.
AI.conclusion: Nimbus Studio reproduced the scientific results of independent reference implementations across datasets, paradigms, validation schemes, conventional and deep-learning methods, and extensibility components. The findings support the platform's numerical and procedural reliability, while the accompanying harness and per-subject results enable independent verification.
